book: 190 - The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned

chapters.relation: Argues that Leia and Padme really are strong feminist characters, using Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex to defuse the two stock objections: Padme's motherhood is 'freely chosen' rather than an oppressive role, and Leia chained in Jabba's palace keeps command of her sexuality, turning the damsel-in-distress plot around by strangling Jabba with her own chain and later rescuing Han herself. The chapter's real complaint is structural: with only six speaking women in the original trilogy, almost all of them royalty, Leia and Padme are forced to represent all women (the 'affluent few' problem), while Shmi, Aunt Beru, Mon Mothma, and the handmaidens Sabe, Corde, and Dorme never get the screen time to show their strength.

Reads Leia's gold-bikini captivity in Jabba's palace as an image of contemporary culture's fear of fat: Jabba, the rancor, and the Sarlaac personify uncontrolled appetite and Sartre's 'slimy' being-in-itself, while Leia's thin, disciplined body epitomizes the anorexic ideal. Drawing on Susan Bordo and Foucault's docile bodies, the chapter argues the scene chains women to a tyrannical ideal of slimness so that Leia herself becomes the oppressor, and closes with Sartre's point that consciousness depends on its body, so we should suspend the fear of flesh and embrace embodied life as the Force does.

Uses the Zillo Beast arc, battle droids, mynocks, and Han shooting Greedo to test theories of moral status: Schweitzer-style reverence for life would forbid a Jedi from eating anything, genetic views breed Palpatine-style human chauvinism, Singer's sentience view makes droid suffering and Luke dropping the rancor's door morally troubling, and Kantian autonomy excludes cognitively impaired beings too harshly. The chapter weighs Palpatine as merely a 'sociopathic' goal-pursuer rather than a Kantian moral agent, and leaves the droid question open via the novel Children of the Jedi, where the droid-converted Nichos lacks even mere agency because he cannot override his programming.

chapters.file: ch27 - Episode V Metaphysics Strikes Back.md

chapters.relation: Asks how an all-encompassing, good Force can have a dark side: after framing the Force as panentheistic, it tests Augustine's privation theory (Alderaan's destruction as an absence of 'measure, order, and form') and a Daoist reading of Yoda's equanimity modeled on Zhuangzi drumming and singing after his wife's death, rejecting both because Vader's evil is active, disciplined, and full of the Force rather than a lack. The answer endorsed is Schelling's: the will needs a dark 'ground' - Yoda's 'anger, fear, aggression' - which is benign when ordered by the will of love and becomes evil when it separatisitically defies it, which is what 'bringing balance to the Force' means.

Reads Jedi training through Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology and the enactivism of Varela, Thompson, and Rosch: Obi-Wan's blast-shield remote drill and Yoda's Dagobah obstacle course work because perception, thought, and action are one embodied flow rather than a perception-cognition-action 'sandwich.' Luke fails to lift the X-wing because his habits do not yet present the ship as liftable, while for Yoda 'size matters not'; and Jedi need no special Force-organ (so midi-chlorians are redundant) because skilled interaction, like Bach-y-Rita's tactile-vision subjects, determines what experience is like.

Asks whether Han Solo's 'hokey religions' dismissal of the Force is unreasonable given his evidence, answering no: Hume's argument against miracles explains why testimony of lightsaber tricks and mind tricks should not overturn Han's experience of consistent natural law, while Hume's problem of induction and custom/habit explain why both Han's 'luck' verdict and Obi-Wan's 'no such thing as luck' are habit-based generalizations. Peirce's fallibilism (backed by Putnam's 'fallibilism does not entail skepticism') lets Han and Obi-Wan each claim knowledge without certainty, echoing Obi-Wan's line that many truths depend greatly on our own point of view.

chapters.file: ch31 - Episode VI Return of the Non-Human.md

chapters.relation: Asks whether droids like C-3PO and R2-D2 can think, staging Searle's Chinese Room as a 'Bocce Room' to argue that droid anxiety, pain, and heroism might be mere input-output symbol shuffling. It then rebuts Searle with the systems reply (the room as a whole, not the person inside, might understand) and a neuron-by-neuron mechanical brain-replacement thought experiment showing the biological/mechanical divide is arbitrary, concluding that restraining bolts, memory wipes, and the Mos Eisley cantina's 'we don't serve their kind here' prejudice lose their justification if droids might genuinely suffer.

Pits Chomsky's structure-based verdict - Chewbacca's roars are unscripted, grammarless animal noises, hence not language - against Wittgenstein's meaning-as-use: the builder's language of 'wrench' and 'hydrospanner' shows that unstructured commands can work perfectly as a language-game. Obi-Wan's private Force-diary symbol 'S' illustrates the private language argument (no standard of correct use without a community), and viewers learn 'Sith,' 'lightsaber,' and Chewie's frustration at the medal ceremony from use alone, so Chewie genuinely communicates despite Shyriiwook having no real-world grammar.

Uses Palpatine's cloning of the last Zillo Beast, Boba Fett's SCNT creation from Jango, and Thrawn's Hand of Thrawn resurrection scheme to argue de-extinction is impossible: if species are individuals (Ghiselin's species nominalism, grounded in Darwinian variation against Aristotle's species essentialism), then extinction closes the species' unique life story, so any clone is a numerically distinct new individual. The same numerical-vs-qualitative identity point shows Thrawn's clone would not be Thrawn, and only Palpatine's dark-side survival in a cloned body - not cloning itself - counts as genuine resurrection.

chapters.file: ch35 - Episode VII The Fandom Awakens.md

chapters.relation: Maps Campbell's Hero's Journey onto Luke's arc in A New Hope (ordinary world, meeting the mentor, crossing the threshold, atonement with the 'Dark Father' Vader), then argues both Campbell and Lucas misunderstand myth: following Malinowski, myth is a living social charter and therefore ideology, so Star Wars' cosmic dualism, male-centered monomyth, and celebration of violence conceal political and commercial power. The chapter's closing turn - 'Star Wars(TM) is the real Empire and the fans its consumer-subjects,' with Reagan's SDI and an 'insurgents vs. Empire' reading of the Rebellion as illustrations - applies ideology-critique to the franchise itself.

Takes the carbon-freezing scene - Leia's 'I love you,' Han's 'I know,' Chewie's howls - to pose the paradox of fiction: we feel genuine, involuntary fear and pity for characters we know do not exist. It tests and rejects the illusion theory (we do not flee Vader's 501st Legion), the thought theory (we pity Han himself, not our mental representation of him), and Walton's pretend theory (viewers' emotions, unlike a child's Darth Maul lightsaber play, are not voluntary), landing on Radford's conclusion that our tears over the binary sunset and Obi-Wan's death are real emotions but not rational ones.

Uses a vintage Blue Snaggletooth action figure to illustrate Dennett's three stances - physical (AFA wear-grading of dented boots), design (why the Sears-exclusive mispack is valuable), and intentional (predicting whether Han would shoot first at a pedant correcting his parsec gaffe) - arguing that play trains a third-person science of mind that Descartes' first-person introspection and dualism could never verify. Dennett's account of religion as a misapplied intentional stance then explains begging the Falcon to 'hold together' and Zeus's lightning as projected intention, with the twist that children playing with figures know they are pretending while the superstitious mind does not.

Analyzes Lucasfilm's April 2014 press release demoting the entire Expanded Universe (including Zahn's Thrawn Trilogy and the slicer Ghent) to noncanonical 'gossip,' contrasting it with the older G-T-C-S-N canon hierarchy and using Barthes' 'Death of the Author' to deny that creators can fix a fiction's meaning. Canon is shown to be dynamic, negotiable, and participatory - Aayla Secura rose from N-Canon to C-Canon after Attack of the Clones, fans picked R4-G9's color, the Holiday Special fell from Gospel - so Lucasfilm cannot unilaterally settle whether Han shot first: 'Star Wars is, after all, about rebellion.'

chapters.file: ch40 - Contributors Troopers of the 501st Legion.md

holes.name: Susan Bordo
holes.what: Contemporary feminist philosopher of the body who analyzes the cultural vilification of fat and the tyrannical 'anorexic aesthetic' of thinness as disciplines imposed on the female body.
holes.why: Chapter 25 explicitly builds its reading of Leia's captivity scene on Bordo's account of the fear of fat alongside Sartre and Foucault, but she has no slug in the taxonomy.

holes.name: F.W.J. Schelling
holes.what: German idealist whose freedom treatise treats evil as a real, dark 'ground' within the divine will that becomes evil when it asserts itself against the will of love.
holes.why: Chapter 28's positive answer to why the Force must have a dark side is essentially Schelling's dark-ground metaphysics, which no existing slug covers.

holes.name: Panentheism
holes.what: The view that everything that exists is encompassed within one divine reality (Brahman, Dao, God, the Force) which nevertheless exceeds the world.
holes.why: Chapter 28 argues the Force is panentheistic and that this very doctrine creates the problem of how a good all-encompassing Force can contain or ground evil.

holes.name: Enactivism
holes.what: 4E-cognition view (Varela, Thompson, Rosch) that perception, thought, and action form one enacted loop - mind is something you do, not a model built between perceiving and acting.
holes.why: Chapter 29 applies the enactivist perception-action loop to Jedi training and the flow of the Force; only Merleau-Ponty's embodiment is covered by the taxonomy.

holes.name: Noam Chomsky
holes.what: Linguist-philosopher who holds that a genuine language requires syntax determined by a generative grammar.
holes.why: Chapter 33 uses Chomsky's structure-based criterion as the foil that rules Chewbacca's roars out of language before Wittgenstein's use-based answer brings them back in.

holes.name: Charles Darwin
holes.what: Naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection makes heritable variation within species fundamental to biology.
holes.why: Chapter 34's argument that species essentialism is false, and hence that de-extinction is impossible, rests entirely on Darwinian natural selection.

holes.name: The Species Problem
holes.what: The philosophy-of-biology puzzle of what individuates a species: fixed essential traits (Aristotelian essentialism) versus historical individuals defined by unique origins (Ghiselin's species nominalism).
holes.why: Chapter 34 is organized around this problem to argue that a cloned Zillo Beast could not resurrect the extinct species.

holes.name: The Monomyth (Hero's Journey)
holes.what: Joseph Campbell's thesis, drawing on Jung, that all world mythologies share a single hero-quest structure of departure, initiation, and return.
holes.why: Chapter 36 maps Luke's arc onto the monomyth stage by stage and then criticizes it as ideology, and no taxonomy slug covers Campbell's framework.

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle that we have genuine emotional responses to characters we know do not exist, given that rational emotion seems to require belief in really existing objects.
holes.why: Chapter 37 structures its entire analysis of grieving at Han's carbon-freezing around this paradox and the failure of the illusion, thought, and pretend theories.

holes.name: Roland Barthes
holes.what: French literary theorist whose 'The Death of the Author' argues that a work's meaning is not fixed by authorial intention or biography.
holes.why: Chapter 39 leans on Barthes to argue that Lucasfilm cannot unilaterally dictate what counts as canonical Star Wars.

holes.name: The Death of the Author
holes.what: Barthes' thesis that interpretation should not privilege the author's intentions, since what readers bring to a text matters equally.
holes.why: Chapter 39 deploys this thesis against Lucasfilm's claim of near-total control over the Star Wars canon after the 2014 Expanded Universe reset.
